p: Jordan learned to read the coded weather reports line by line, remarks and all.
On a gusty May morning she canceled her own lesson before Abby said a word, and the wind showed up right when the forecast said it would.
She told Russ what the weather advisories said about his mountain route, and he moved his trip.
On a trampoline at Claire's she explained to Ellie why clouds have flat bottoms.
In June a thunderstorm built over the Palmer Divide during a lesson. Jordan turned for home, landed before it hit, and read Claire and Ellie Danny's page about the day he got Zulu time wrong.
Marisol Tran. The mechanic, who would rather fix a thing now than later.
Russ Kim. A partner, and the loudest voice in the club chat.
Walt Herrera. Still checking her logbook every month.
Lourdes Reyes. Jordan's mother, who worries out loud.

The sectional had been sitting on top of Jordan's refrigerator for three weeks, still in its plastic sleeve, next to a bag of coffee filters and a fire extinguisher she'd bought the same day for the same reason. Things a responsible person owns.

Abby had brought it up on the ramp the week of the storm, deadpan, a coffee in each hand. Denver's Class B was a wedding cake upside down, and Jordan was going to learn every layer. Bring the sectional you bought and haven't opened. Jordan hadn't asked how she knew.

Tuesday she came off a twenty four hour shift at seven in the morning, slept until one, and ate cereal standing up at the counter. Then she got the sectional down and wrestled it out of the plastic. It unfolded, and unfolded, and kept going, and when it quit it was roughly a twin sheet with print on both sides and Denver hanging off the table into her lap.

It took her a minute to find home. Denver was a yellow splotch, spilled lemonade. Denver International was out east, a snarl of blue and magenta with runways sticking out of it like straws. And twenty miles south southwest, on the bottom edge of the yellow, a little blue circle with runways in it and CENTENNIAL in small type, sitting in the middle of a nest of blue lines like a bird nobody told about the nest.
She got a pen and a legal pad and did what she always did with something she didn't understand. She wrote down exactly what she saw, before she let herself decide what any of it meant.

Jordan's notes on the chart around Centennial, Tuesday. One: solid blue rings and wedges centered on Denver International, each with a blue fraction, a top number and a bottom number. Over Centennial the bottom number is 80. Two: a dashed blue line around Centennial itself, and next to it a tiny box with a minus sign and 80. Three: way out, a thin magenta circle around the whole city, printed Mode C and A D S B Out, thirty N M. Centennial is well inside it. Four: out east, a fuzzy magenta band, like somebody traced a line with a highlighter and smudged it. Five: above Denver International, in small type, N O, S V F R. Six: I have no idea what any of this means. Abby says it's a wedding cake.
She took a picture of the legal pad and texted it to Abby.
A text from Abby Strand. Good list. Number 1 is the only one that can end my career. Saturday 7am. Briefing room. Bring the chart and the list.
Then a minute later, a second bubble: Also there's a chart of Danny's in Biscuit's seat back. Out of date. Don't fly with it. You'll want to see it though.

Jordan sat there with the chart in her lap for a while. Then she drove to the airport, because it wasn't even three yet, and found it where Abby said. A Denver sectional eight years out of date, from the summer of 2018, folded soft as cloth along the creases, with a coffee ring on Castle Rock and pencil lines out to Akron and Moab and Steamboat. On the Denver panel, the little blue 80 over Centennial had been circled in red pen. Circled three times, hard enough that the pen had gone through the paper on the last lap.
Next to it, in his block capitals: 80!!!
She didn't know what it meant. She put it in her flight bag anyway.
Abby's Ground School: who owns the sky, and how to ask them.
The alphabet, and who's in charge of it.

Unfold the whole thing. Yes, all of it. Weigh the corners down with the coffee cups, and if you knock mine over, you're buying the next one. Today's the day the colors on that chart stop being decoration. Every line on there is a rule somebody can enforce, and the FAA has a whole office whose job is drawing them.

Start with the big split. Controlled airspace is Classes A, B, C, D, and E. That's where air traffic control provides service, and depending on the class, where you need to talk to them, be equipped for them, or have their permission. Uncontrolled airspace is Class G. Nobody's controlling traffic in Class G, but the weather minimums still apply there, and so does every other rule in Part 91. Uncontrolled doesn't mean lawless. It means you're the controller.

Class A runs from 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL600, and everything in it flies IFR. It isn't even drawn on your sectional, because no VFR pilot is supposed to be there. Biscuit couldn't get there on a good day with a tailwind and a prayer, so we'll leave it there.

Class E is everything controlled that isn't A, B, C, or D. Where the chart doesn't say otherwise, it starts at 14,500 feet MSL. But almost nowhere is otherwise. Over most of the country it starts 1,200 feet above the ground. Around airports with instrument approaches it comes down to 700 feet, and the chart shows that with a fuzzy magenta band, the vignette, which is item 4 on your list. Where the floor is something other than 700 and it borders Class G, the band is blue. Some airports have Class E right down to the surface, drawn with a dashed magenta line. Above FL600 it's Class E again, which you will never need to know except on a test.

Class G is whatever's left, from the ground up to wherever the Class E starts over your head. Out on the eastern plains, away from everything, you can be in Class G right up to 700 or 1,200 feet above the wheat.

How the exam asks it. Know the vertical limits of each class and how each one is drawn. Class E floors at 700 AGL (magenta vignette), 1,200 AGL (blue vignette next to Class G), the surface (dashed magenta), or 14,500 MSL where nothing else is charted.
Class B: the upside down wedding cake.

Item 1 on your list. Class B surrounds the busiest airports in the country, and it's built in layers. A surface area around the main airport, then shelves that get wider and higher as you go out, so the whole thing looks like a wedding cake somebody flipped over. The AIM really does call it that. It's shaped that way to keep the airliners inside it all the way down to the runway.

Each layer gets a blue fraction on the chart. The top number is the ceiling and the bottom number is the floor, both in hundreds of feet MSL. So 80 on the bottom means the floor of that shelf is 8,000 feet above sea level. Not above the ground. Sea level. Now look where that 80 sits. Right over us. The FAA's own Centennial pilot page says it in one sentence: the base of the Denver Class B over Centennial is 8,000. Our field is 5,885. Do the subtraction. That's about 2,100 feet of sky between our runways and the bottom of the most regulated airspace in the region. You'll be climbing through that in under five minutes every single time you leave here, and the shelf is sitting right there waiting for you to get distracted.

Here's the rule that matters most in this whole chapter. You need an ATC clearance to enter Class B. Every time, no matter the weather. That's 91.131(a)(1). And a clearance has words. The controller will say your call sign and cleared to enter the Bravo airspace, or cleared through the Bravo airspace. If you didn't hear those words, you aren't cleared. Radar contact is not a clearance. A squawk code is not a clearance. Flight following is not a clearance. Being handed off from the tower to Approach and having a nice conversation with them is not a clearance. And if ATC gives you a heading or an altitude that would put you inside without saying the words, you say so. Their own rulebook says a VFR pilot is expected to speak up if an instruction would make them break a regulation. If you're not sure, you're not cleared. Ask.

To fly in it at all, the airplane needs a two way radio, a transponder with Mode C altitude reporting, and ADS-B Out. The pilot needs at least a private certificate, or, for a student, 61.95. That means ground and flight training from an instructor on that specific Class B, with the flight training done in it, and a logbook endorsement from that instructor, dated within the 90 days before the flight, saying you're proficient to solo in that specific Class B. Taking off or landing at an airport inside Class B takes its own endorsement for that airport. And there's a list of twelve airports in Appendix D, section 4 where solo students can't take off or land at all, period. Atlanta, O'Hare, LAX, the New York ones, a few others. Denver International isn't on it. You still aren't going there.

VFR inside Class B is 3 miles visibility and clear of clouds, and ATC separates you from other traffic while you're in it. Under a Class B shelf, or in a VFR corridor through one, the speed limit is 200 knots indicated, 91.117(c). Everywhere below 10,000 MSL it's 250. Biscuit couldn't do 200 if you dropped her off a cliff. The test asks anyway.

One more thing from the AIM, and I want you to take it personally. It cautions VFR pilots against flying too close to Class B boundaries, especially where the floor is low or close to the altitudes people like to cruise at. That's us. My rule is I stay at least 300 feet under any floor I'm not cleared into. Make it your rule too, until you make a better one.

How the exam asks it. Class B needs a clearance, a two way radio, a Mode C transponder, and ADS-B Out. VFR minimums are 3 SM and clear of clouds. Students need a 61.95 endorsement within 90 days. The speed limit under a shelf is 200 knots.
The veil, the transponder, and ADS-B Out.

Item 3. That thin magenta circle is the Mode C veil. It's 30 nautical miles around every airport listed in Appendix D, section 1 of Part 91, which is mostly the Class B airports, and Denver International is on the list. Inside it, from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL, every airplane needs a transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out. That's 91.215(b)(2) and 91.225(d)(2). We're about 20 miles from Denver International. We are in the veil sitting on the ramp with the engine off.

The same equipment is required in Class A, B, and C, and above the ceiling of a Class B or C area within its lateral limits, up to 10,000 MSL. And everywhere in the lower 48 at and above 10,000 MSL, except within 2,500 feet of the ground. That exception matters out here. Out past the veil, climb to 10,500 over the foothills, and if the terrain under you is within 2,500 feet, the 10,000 foot rule doesn't apply right there. ADS-B adds one area the transponder rule doesn't have: over the Gulf, at and above 3,000 MSL, out to 12 miles from the coast. The one exemption is for aircraft that were never certificated with an engine driven electrical system, plus balloons and gliders. They can be in the veil as long as they stay out of the Class B and C and below their ceilings or 10,000, whichever is lower. Biscuit has an alternator, so that's not us.

Transponders answer radar. ADS-B Out is different. It's the airplane broadcasting its own GPS position and velocity, over and over, to anybody listening, ground stations and other airplanes. It has to transmit at all times, 91.225(f), unless ATC tells you otherwise. Below 18,000 feet either of the two approved systems is legal. Class A requires the 1090 megahertz version. Marisol and Danny installed Biscuit's box in 2019, before the January 1, 2020 deadline, and Marisol will tell you how many weekends that took if you buy her lunch.

VFR, you squawk 1200 unless ATC gives you something else, with altitude reporting on. 7700 is an emergency. 7600 means you've lost your radio. If something's broken, there are deviation rules: if the transponder or ADS-B quits, you can ask ATC at any time to fly to your destination or to a repair shop. If the airplane isn't equipped at all, you ask at least an hour before. The AIM says the ADS-B request goes through an FAA web tool, between one and 24 hours ahead. And any of those is permission you ask for. It isn't something you get to assume.

How the exam asks it. Transponder with Mode C and ADS-B Out: Class A, B, C, the 30 NM veil to 10,000 MSL, above B and C ceilings to 10,000, and at and above 10,000 MSL in the 48 states except within 2,500 AGL. 1200 VFR, 7600 lost comm, 7700 emergency.
Class C and Class D: say my name.

Class C first, even though we don't have one. Colorado Springs does. It's typically a 5 mile core from the surface up to 4,000 feet above the airport, and a 10 mile shelf from 1,200 feet up to 4,000 above the airport, all charted in MSL and drawn in solid magenta. There's also an outer area, normally 20 miles, that isn't charted. There's no pilot certificate requirement. You need a two way radio, a Mode C transponder, and ADS-B Out, and you need to establish two way radio communication before you go in. Inside, ATC separates VFR traffic from IFR traffic.

Class D is what we live in. It's usually from the surface up to 2,500 feet above the airport, charted in MSL, around an airport with an operating control tower. It's the dashed blue line, item 2 on your list, and the little box is the ceiling in hundreds of feet. The minus sign means up to but not including. So minus 80 means our Class D runs from the surface up to but not including 8,000 MSL, which is exactly where the Class B floor starts. They stacked them like Legos. Centennial's tower runs 24 hours. Some don't. Rocky Mountain Metro's tower runs six in the morning until ten at night, and when a part time tower closes, the airspace turns into Class E or Class G. The Chart Supplement says which.

Now the rule for C and D, and it's a sneaky one. You need two way radio communication established before you enter. Established means the controller answered you with your call sign. Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, standby: you're established, you can go in. Aircraft calling Centennial Tower, standby: you are not, because they didn't say who they were talking to. Cessna Niner One Echo, remain outside the Class Delta: you're established and you've been told to stay out, so you stay out. That's straight from the AIM. The test loves it, and so do I.

At any airport with an operating tower, you need a clearance to taxi, take off, or land, 91.129(i). At or below 2,500 feet above the ground within 4 miles of the main airport of a Class C or D, the speed limit is 200 knots. And if you're flying to a towered airport that sits in Class E or G, you still have to talk to the tower, and 91.126 and 91.127 say you establish that before you're 4 miles out, up to and including 2,500 feet above the ground. One more thing about Class D: the tower sequences you to the runway, but it doesn't separate VFR traffic for you. Your eyes do that.

How the exam asks it. If the controller uses your call sign, communication is established, even with "standby." If they don't, or they say remain outside, you stay out. Class C and D speed limit within 4 NM, at or below 2,500 AGL: 200 knots.
How far from the clouds, and how far you can see.

Now 91.155, basic VFR weather minimums. This is the table everybody memorizes and then forgets on a gray morning. Visibility is how far you can see ahead. Cloud clearance is how far you stay from the clouds, below, above, and sideways. Here it is.

Class A doesn't apply, you're not there. In Class B airspace it's 3 statute miles and clear of clouds. Class C airspace, Class D airspace, and Class E airspace below 10,000 MSL are all the same: 3 miles, and 500 feet below the clouds, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal. People call that three one five two. Three miles, one thousand above, five hundred below, two thousand sideways. Class E at or above 10,000 MSL gets stricter because everybody's going faster up there: 5 miles, 1,000 below, 1,000 above, and a mile horizontal.

Class G airspace has three bands, and the test lives in them. At or below 1,200 feet above the surface, no matter the MSL altitude, it's 1 mile and clear of clouds by day, and three one five two at night. More than 1,200 above the surface but below 10,000 MSL, it's 1 mile by day and 3 at night, and both use the 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal clearances. More than 1,200 above the surface and at or above 10,000 MSL, it's 5 miles and 1,000, 1,000, and a mile, same as Class E up there. There's one night exception for airplanes in Class G under 1,200 AGL: in a traffic pattern within half a mile of the runway, you can go clear of clouds with 1 mile.
Think about where we live. Field elevation is 5,885. Ten thousand MSL is barely 4,100 feet over the airport. Over the mountains, you hit the 10,000 foot rules before you've cleared the foothills.

Two more out of 91.155, both about airports. You can't fly VFR beneath a ceiling of less than 1,000 feet within the surface area of controlled airspace. And you can't take off, land, or enter the pattern in a Class B, C, D, or E surface area unless the ground visibility is at least 3 miles. If there's no ground visibility reported, then the flight visibility has to be 3. Our Class D is a surface area. So two and a half miles in smoke, and nobody from this airport is leaving VFR.

Unless they ask for Special VFR. That's 91.157. Inside the surface area, below 10,000 MSL, with an ATC clearance, you can go clear of clouds with 1 mile of flight visibility, and you need 1 mile of ground visibility to take off or land. At night it's only for instrument rated pilots in airplanes equipped for IFR. It isn't allowed at all at the airports in Appendix D, section 3, and Denver International is one of them. That's your item 5, NO SVFR over the airport name. I'll be honest about Special VFR. It's legal, and it's also how good pilots end up running into clouds they couldn't see coming at a mile. Biscuit and I don't do it with students.

How the exam asks it. Expect the table, especially Class G by day and night and the change at 10,000 MSL. Expect 91.155(c) and (d) and the Special VFR requirements. Know the 1,200 AGL break is measured above the surface.
Special use airspace, and the other stuff on the chart.

Special use airspace is where something's going on that the rest of us need to stay out of or watch out for. Two kinds are regulatory, written into Part 73. Prohibited areas, marked P and a number, you don't fly in. Period. The PHAK uses P-40 at Camp David. Restricted areas, R and a number, have invisible hazards like artillery, aerial gunnery, and missiles. When they're active, you don't go in without permission from the using or controlling agency, 91.133. When they're inactive and released to the FAA, IFR traffic can get routed through.

The rest are nonregulatory, which means warnings, and you ignore them at your own risk. Warning areas, W, start 3 miles off the coast and cover the same kind of hazards out over the water. Military operations areas have names, not numbers, and they're there to keep military training away from IFR traffic. VFR, you're allowed in one, but if it's active you can meet fighters doing aerobatics at well over 250 knots, so you call the controlling agency or any Flight Service station within 100 miles for the status. Alert areas, A, mean lots of training or unusual flying, and everybody in there is equally responsible for not hitting each other. Controlled firing areas aren't charted at all, because they stop shooting the second anyone sees an airplane coming. National security areas ask you to avoid them voluntarily, and they can be made temporarily prohibited by NOTAM when the government needs that. The chart margins list the special use areas with their altitudes, hours, and who controls them.

Then other airspace. Military training routes are low, fast highways for military jets, mostly below 10,000 MSL at speeds over 250 knots. IR routes are flown IFR, VR routes VFR. Four digits means no segment of it goes above 1,500 feet AGL. Three digits means at least one segment does. Terminal radar service areas are drawn with a black outline, and using them is voluntary. There are parachute jump areas, published VFR routes, and VFR flyways on the back of terminal area charts. You'll see some of each before you're done.

Three kinds of numbers on the sectional that the test loves to show you in a picture. A tower or an antenna gets a little upside down V with two numbers next to it. The bold one on top is the top of the obstruction in feet above sea level. The one in parentheses under it is its height above the ground. Big number with a small one after it, in the middle of a grid square, is the maximum elevation figure, the highest thing in that square plus some margin, in thousands and hundreds of feet MSL. And every airport has a data block. Name, then the identifier, then the tower frequency if it has one, then a line with the field elevation, an L if the lights are on from sunset to sunrise, the longest runway in hundreds of feet, and the CTAF. A C in a circle next to a frequency means that's the common traffic advisory frequency, the one you talk on when there's no tower or the tower's closed.

The chart also tells you about the ground itself, once you learn the colors. Terrain is drawn with contour lines, thin lines joining points at the same elevation, and the closer together they run, the steeper the ground. Between them the chart is shaded with elevation tints, pale green for the lowest land and on through tan and brown as it climbs, and the legend in the margin gives the elevation for each color. Hilltops and peaks get a spot elevation, a dot with a number in feet MSL. The maximum elevation figure in each square covers all of it, terrain and towers both. On our sectional the plains east of Centennial are pale. Look west and the colors go dark inside twenty miles. That's the Front Range telling you to pay attention.
How the exam asks it. Match each special use area to its letter and what it means for a VFR pilot. Prohibited and restricted are regulatory. Know the MTR numbering rule and that CFAs aren't charted.
TFRs and NOTAMs: the airspace that isn't on the chart.

Your sectional is printed every 56 days. The sky changes faster than that. NOTAM is short for Notice to Airmen, and it's how the FAA tells you about everything temporary: closed runways, broken navaids, cranes, airshows, and airspace that didn't exist yesterday. 91.103 says you become familiar with all available information before a flight, and NOTAMs are information. You'll get them from Flight Service, from NOTAM Search on the FAA's site, or from a flight planning app that pulls them in.

There are a few classes. NOTAM D is the everyday kind, for airports, runways, taxiways, lighting, navaids, and general airspace activity. FDC NOTAMs are regulatory: changes to instrument procedures and charts, high barometric pressure warnings, laser activity, and temporary flight restrictions. Pointer NOTAMs point to other NOTAMs. There are international and military ones too.

A TFR is issued as an FDC NOTAM, and there are rules behind each type. 91.137 covers disasters and hazards. Under (a)(1), it's a hazard on the surface, a gas leak, say, and only relief aircraft under the direction of the official in charge get to go in. Under (a)(2), it's to give disaster relief aircraft room to work, like air tankers on a fire. There's a short list of who else can be in there: aircraft carrying law enforcement, IFR flights approved by ATC, flights going straight to or from an airport inside the area, or that have to cross it because weather or terrain makes going around impracticable, after notifying the facility named in the NOTAM and never to look at the disaster, and accredited news media with a flight plan, flying above the relief aircraft. Sightseers are not on the list. Under (a)(3), it's to keep sightseers from piling up over something newsworthy. 91.141 is the President, the Vice President, and other public figures. 91.143 is space launches. 91.144 is barometric pressure over 31 inches. 91.145 covers airshows and major sporting events. For an aerial demonstration it's normally 5 miles around, and for a sporting event 3 miles and 2,500 feet above the surface, with the NOTAM out at least 30 days ahead.

Here's the trap. Only national security TFRs are drawn on the sectional. The rest you have to go look up, every time. The PHAK says it plainly: pilots who bust TFRs have ended up in security investigations and with certificate suspensions. When you read one, find the center point, the radius, the altitudes, the times in Zulu, who's in charge, and who to call. Then draw it on your chart in pencil and give it room.
How the exam asks it. TFRs are FDC NOTAMs. Know which section covers which kind. Most TFRs are not charted, so checking NOTAMs is part of preflight under 91.103.

The radio scares everybody for about ten flights. Then it's just a phone call where everybody talks too fast. The AIM gives you the format for a first call to anybody: who you're calling, who you are, where you are, and what you want. Centennial's own FAA page says what Ground wants from a VFR airplane: call sign, type, that you're VFR, the direction you want to go, and the ATIS letter. So it sounds like this. Centennial Ground, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, at Hangar Six, VFR eastbound, with Lima. That's it. They'll do the rest.

Your call sign is the type and the numbers. When you say Cessna, you drop the N. You never shorten it on the first call. After the controller shortens it, you can too, and the short version is the type and the last three, Cessna Niner One Echo. If two call signs on the frequency sound alike, use the whole thing and make them use it too.

Numbers. Nine is niner. Altitudes are said in thousands and hundreds, seven thousand five hundred, and anything at ten thousand or more gets the digits split, one zero thousand five hundred. A decimal in a frequency is point. Headings are three digits, heading zero niner zero. Time on the radio is Zulu unless somebody says local.

Read back runway assignments, hold short instructions, and anything with a number in it. Controllers are required to get a readback of every runway hold short instruction, so you might as well give it to them the first time. Two phrases at Centennial get people in trouble. Monitor Tower means switch to the tower frequency and listen. It does not mean call them, and it is not a clearance onto the runway. And line up and wait means taxi onto the runway and sit there. It is not a takeoff clearance. Taxi instructions to a runway don't let you onto that runway either. You hold short until somebody tells you otherwise.

Last one. Sooner or later a controller may say this to you: your call sign, then possible pilot deviation, advise you contact, then a facility, at, then a phone number. Pilots call it the Brasher warning, after a court case. It's in the controllers' rulebook word for word. It means they think you broke a rule, and they're giving you a chance to write it down while it's fresh. If you ever hear it, fly the airplane first. Acknowledge it, write the number down, and get on the ground. Don't argue on frequency. Then calm down and call. Then file a report with NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System. Under AC 00-46F, if you get that report in within 10 days after the event, or after you realized it happened, and it was inadvertent, didn't involve a crime or an accident, and you haven't had a violation in the last five years, the FAA can still find a violation but it won't fine you or suspend your certificate. Walt has forms. Of course Walt has forms.

Don't mix that 10 days up with the other 10 days in aviation. The NASA report is for things like an airspace bust. If there's an accident, somebody badly hurt or the airplane seriously damaged, a NASA report doesn't protect you at all. That's the NTSB's rule, 49 CFR 830. It says you notify the NTSB immediately, and then the written report is due within 10 days. We'll do the whole list before your written. For now, keep the split straight. NASA is about protecting you after a mistake. The NTSB is about finding out what happened.

Before you call anybody, you listen. At a towered airport the ATIS, the automatic terminal information service, is a recording on its own frequency with the weather, the runway in use, the altimeter setting, and any notices that matter today. Each new recording gets the next letter, information Lima, then Mike, and it's updated at least every hour, sooner if something changes. Telling Ground you have Lima saves everybody thirty seconds. Airports without ATIS often have an automated weather station instead. ASOS is the bigger automated surface observing system, and AWOS is its smaller cousin, some of them owned by the airport. ASOS and the bigger AWOS sets read out wind, visibility, sky, temperature, dewpoint, and altimeter on a frequency. The smallest AWOS may give you only the altimeter, so listen for what's missing. Most have a phone number in the Chart Supplement. Remember what it is, though. A computer reporting what one sensor sees right now, at one spot on the field. It doesn't know about the snow shower two miles away.
How the exam asks it. Expect a question on the order of an initial call, on abbreviating call signs, on what "line up and wait" allows, and on the protection a timely NASA report gives you.
When the radio quits: light gun signals.

Every tower has a light gun, a big spotlight that can shine red, green, or white at one airplane. It's for airplanes with no radio, or airplanes whose radio quit. The light gun signals are in 91.125, and you're going to memorize them because the test will absolutely ask.

On the ground: steady green is cleared for takeoff. Flashing green is cleared to taxi. Steady red is stop. Flashing red is taxi clear of the runway in use. Flashing white is return to your starting point on the airport. In the air: steady green is cleared to land. Flashing green is return for landing, and a steady green will follow when it's time. Steady red is give way to other aircraft and keep circling. Flashing red is airport unsafe, do not land. Flashing white in the air doesn't mean anything. Alternating red and green, anywhere, is exercise extreme caution.
In the air by day, rock your wings. On the ground by day, move your ailerons or rudder. At night, either way, blink your landing or nav lights.

If you lose the radio in our Class D, 91.129(d) says you can still come in and land if the weather's at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you get a clearance to land, which here means a steady green. Squawk 7600 so the radar people know what's going on. And before you decide the radio is dead, check the dumb stuff: the volume, the squelch, the headset plugs, the frequency you dialed, the push to talk switch. Half of the radio failures I've had were me.

How the exam asks it. The full light gun table, ground and air. Flashing white has no meaning in flight. Lost comm VFR into Class D: VFR weather, visual contact with the tower, and a clearance to land.

Saturday at seven the briefing room smelled like burnt coffee and the dry erase markers somebody had left uncapped all week. Abby had taped Jordan's new sectional to the wall over the whiteboard, flat, with blue painter's tape at the corners. She didn't say good morning. She tapped the blue 80 over Centennial with a pen.
This one. What is it, and what does it mean for us in about four minutes after takeoff?
Jordan had Danny's old chart in her flight bag, folded to the same panel, with the same number circled in red three times. She didn't take it out.
Over Centennial, the sectional shows a blue 80. What does it tell Jordan?
A. The Class B ends at 8,000 feet, and above that, they can fly freely.
B. The Class B floor is 8,000 MSL, and at or above it she needs a clearance.
C. The Class B floor is 8,000 MSL, and at or above it she must be talking to Approach.
D. The Class B starts 8,000 feet above the ground, with plenty of room under it.

The floor of the Bravo. Eight thousand. At or above it I need a clearance. Yep. Eight thousand above sea level, which is about twenty one hundred feet over our heads right now. She draws a line on the whiteboard for the runway, then a lid over it. Climb out east, look at a pretty reservoir, look back at your altimeter, and you're inside the most expensive airspace in Colorado. I've seen students do it in a Cessna with an instructor sitting right there. I've seen instructors do it.

That's it. Class B floors and ceilings are in hundreds of feet MSL, bottom number floor, top number ceiling. Over Centennial the floor is 8,000 MSL, only about 2,100 feet above the field. Entry at or above it takes an ATC clearance under 91.131.

Abby went through the whole cake, layer by layer, drawing it from the side on the whiteboard in blue marker until it looked like a stack of pancakes somebody had dropped. Jordan asked the question she'd been holding since Tuesday.
After I solo. Could I ever fly up there by myself? Through the Bravo, over Denver International. Just to see it.
Abby capped the marker and looked at her for a second, like she was deciding which answer to give and then deciding to give the real one.
Under 14 CFR 61.95, can a student pilot ever solo in Denver's Class B?
A. Yes, with training in it and an instructor endorsement within 90 days.
B. No. A student can't solo in any Class B until she's certificated.
C. Yes, once she's passed the knowledge test and knows the airspace rules.
D. Yes, once Denver Approach clears her in, with nothing else required.

Yes. With three things. Ground and flight training on Denver's Bravo, the flying done in it, and my signature in your logbook within the last ninety days saying you can solo in it. Taking off or landing at an airport inside it takes another one for that airport. She smiles, which is rare enough that Jordan notices. Danny asked me the same thing once, years after his checkride. I wasn't his instructor. I told him to go buy his instructor a burrito.

Yep. That's the one. 61.95: ground and flight training from an authorized instructor on that specific Class B, flight training received in it, and a logbook endorsement dated within the preceding 90 days for solo in that airspace. The same rule adds a separate endorsement for an airport inside it.

Sunday morning, before a lesson, Jordan turned the master on for the preflight and a small amber light lit up on the panel next to the transponder. ADS-B. The label under it, in Marisol's label maker capitals, said FAULT.

Marisol was across the ramp with her head in someone else's cowling. Abby's text said she was fifteen minutes out. The sky was perfect, a calm blue morning, the windsock hanging straight down like it had given up on life.
Jordan looked at the light. The transponder itself was fine. It showed 1200 and the little reply light blinked when she pressed the test.
The ADS-B annunciator reads FAULT on a perfect morning under the Mode C veil. What should Jordan do?
A. Show Marisol the light, and keep Biscuit on the ground until it's fixed.
B. Call Denver Approach and ask for a deviation to fly today's lesson without it.
C. Stay below 8,000 and out of the Class B, where the ADS-B rule doesn't apply.
D. Fly the lesson. The transponder works and reports altitude, and that covers the veil.

Marisol comes over wiping her hands, looks at the light, and sighs through her nose. Ten minutes later she's on her back under the panel with a flashlight in her teeth. GPS antenna connector. Backed off. The box can't tell anybody where it is if it doesn't know where it is. She reseats it, safety wires it, and the light goes out. Then she sits on the wing for a minute. Danny and I put this thing in the fall of 2019. Every Saturday in October. He kept saying they'd push the deadline. They didn't. They're wheels up forty minutes late. Abby doesn't mention it.

Exactly right. ADS-B Out is required in the veil, and an annunciated fault means you don't know what the airplane is broadcasting. Ground it, tell the mechanic, and fly when it's fixed. Inoperative equipment that a rule requires can't be deferred with a placard.
The next Saturday was all radio. Abby said so on the walk out. You make every call today. Ground, Tower, Approach, all of it. I'm going to sit here and be a passenger with opinions.

Jordan had the ATIS written on her kneeboard: Information Lima, wind calm, runway 35R in use. She had a script written under it, then crossed it out, then written it again. Her thumb was on the push to talk switch. On a medical channel she could talk a crew through a cardiac arrest without thinking. She had no idea why this was harder.
Whenever you're ready. They're not going anywhere.
Which initial call to Centennial Ground has everything the AIM format asks for?
A. "Centennial Ground, Cessna Niner One Echo, ready to taxi to the active runway."
B. "Ground, this is Biscuit at Hangar Six, we're a student pilot, we'd like to go east today."
C. "Centennial Ground, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, at Hangar Six, ready to taxi."
D. "Centennial Ground, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo at Hangar Six, VFR eastbound with Lima."

Centennial Ground, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo at Hangar Six, VFR eastbound with Lima. Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, Centennial Ground, runway three five right, taxi via Alpha. Advise run up complete. She reads it back, the runway and the taxiway and the call sign, and he says readback correct like it's nothing. Like she does this. Abby gives her a thumbs up without looking over, which somehow counts more.

That's it. Who you're calling, your full call sign, where you are, what you want, and the ATIS. It's the AIM format, and it's what Centennial's FAA page says Ground wants from a VFR airplane. One clean call, one clean answer.
The run up went fine. Jordan called it complete. Ground came back fast.
Cessna Niner One Echo, hold short runway three five right at Alpha, monitor Tower.

She read back the hold short, dialed the tower frequency off her kneeboard, switched over, and rolled up to the hold short line. Four yellow stripes, two solid and two dashed, solid on her side. Tower was a mess. A jet checking in from the north. A helicopter with a long request about the reservoir. Some guy asking about fuel prices, on tower, like it was a drive thru. The runway just sat there in front of her, empty, pointed at the mountains. Nobody said Niner One Echo.
What does Ground's instruction to monitor Tower ask of Jordan?
A. Hold short and listen on the tower frequency until the tower calls Niner One Echo.
B. Stay on Ground's frequency until somebody there tells her to switch over.
C. Taxi onto the runway and line up. Monitor means the tower's planning to clear her next.
D. Call Tower and tell them she's holding short of three five right at Alpha, ready to go.

She sits on the brakes. Two minutes, about. A Citation lands and turns off. A Cirrus goes off the left side. Then: Cessna Niner One Echo, runway three five right, cleared for takeoff, right turn eastbound approved. She reads it back a little too fast, lines up, and pushes the throttle in. Door pops at rotation, like always. She's latched it and is trimming for the climb before it occurs to her that her hand did that on its own.

Yep. That's the one. Monitor means switch frequencies and listen. It's not a request to call and it's not a clearance. Ground told you to hold short, you read it back, and the tower will call you when it wants you.

After an hour over the plains the radio had stopped being terrifying and started being annoying. Abby said that was the correct order. Coming home, she listened to the ATIS, wrote it down, and called the tower about twelve miles east of the airport, outside the dashed blue line, at 7,500, under the shelf.
Centennial Tower, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, one two miles east, seven thousand five hundred, landing with Mike.
The reply came after a few seconds, clipped and busy.
At a hundred knots the edge of the Class D was about three minutes away.
Tower said standby, but didn't name anyone. What should Jordan do before she reaches the Class D?
A. Keep heading in, with the tower's answer counting as two way contact.
B. Drop low and slip in under the Class D to get closer to the airport.
C. Turn away and stay outside the Class D until she hears her call sign.
D. Key the mic again right away and repeat her full call sign for the tower.

Left turn. Outside the dashed line. One lap over a feedlot. You can smell a feedlot from 7,500 feet, it turns out. Ninety seconds. Then: Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, Centennial Tower, enter right downwind runway three five right. Now she's established. She reads it back and goes in. Abby, while Jordan's busy: Half my students hear standby and think it means come on in.

Exactly right. Two way communication requires the controller to use your call sign. Until they do, stay outside the Class D. If they had said your call sign and "standby," you'd be established. If they said "remain outside," you'd stay out.
Decision seven. Two and a half miles.

On the first of July a fire started in the foothills west of Sedalia, southwest of the airport, and by the second the whole south end of the metro was the color of weak tea. Jordan could smell it from her driveway in Aurora at five in the morning. The sun came up red and stayed red.
Centennial, Thursday, 6:53 AM. Wind two one zero at six. Visibility two and a half miles in smoke. Scattered at fifteen thousand. Eighteen and six, altimeter thirty twenty two.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Mija the fire is on channel 9. Tell me you are not flying in that smoke.
The lesson was at seven. Abby hadn't texted. Jordan had learned what that meant.
Centennial's METAR shows two and a half miles in smoke. What should Jordan decide?
A. Drive in and wait at the airport. If the METAR goes to three miles, take off right away.
B. Cancel. The field is under three miles, and 91.155(d) needs three to depart VFR.
C. Go. Two and a half miles is close to three, and it'll be clearer out east of the smoke.
D. Ask the tower for a Special VFR clearance, with its one mile visibility minimum.

She texts Abby: Canceling. KAPA 2 1/2 in smoke. 91.155(d), under 3 in the surface area. Abby: Agree. Then: You quoted a regulation at me before 7 am. I'm putting that on my résumé. Jordan texts her mother: Not flying. Smoke. Going back to bed. Three dots for a long time. Then: Good girl. Jordan is thirty five years old and it still lands somewhere.

That's it. Ground visibility under 3 SM in the Class D surface area means no VFR departure. Smoke also lowers visibility unevenly and hides terrain, other airplanes, and the fire aircraft working nearby.
Friday night the club chat went off like a car alarm.
A message from Russ Kim. swapped myself into biscuit sat 7-9. taking my nephew to see the fire, it's the coolest thing in colorado right now. jordan you can have sun, sun is better anyway
A message from Russ Kim. before anyone says it yes there's a tfr. it's a tfr, not a wall
A message from Walt Herrera. Calendar is first come. Who booked Saturday?
Jordan had booked Saturday on the 20th of June. She had also, an hour earlier, pulled the NOTAMs for the weekend, because now she couldn't not.

The TFR, pulled Friday at 7:04 PM. NOTAM FDC six slash four four seven one, under section 91.137, paragraph a 2: a temporary flight restriction to keep the air safe for firefighting aircraft, five miles around a point eight miles west of Sedalia, from the surface to eleven thousand five hundred MSL. The Douglas County Sheriff runs the emergency response on scene, and Denver Center is the FAA's coordinator. It's in effect from July 1 at eighteen hundred Zulu to July 12 at twenty three fifty nine Zulu.
Russ swapped into Jordan's Saturday slot to show his nephew the fire under a TFR. What should Jordan do?
A. Tell Russ he can go if he stays clear of the tankers and keeps his transponder on.
B. Text the NOTAM to Walt privately as safety officer and let him handle Russ.
C. Let Russ have the Saturday slot and stay out of the TFR question.
D. Post the NOTAM in the club chat, citing the 91.137(a)(2) limits on who can enter.

She pastes the NOTAM text in, then: That's a 91.137(a)(2) for fire aircraft. Sightseeing isn't one of the exceptions. 5 mile radius, surface to 11,500. Also I booked Saturday back on June 20. Happy to trade for Sunday if you want it for something else. Four minutes of nothing. Then Russ: ok first of all who keeps teaching her to read. Walt: Still nobody. Russ: fine. sunday. we'll look at it from i-25 like normal people. 5 miles is a lot of miles. Walt: 5 miles is the TFR. Give it more. Marisol posts a photo of a box of donuts with a sticky note on it that says RUSS OWES.

Yep. That's the one. The NOTAM settles the safety question and the calendar settles the schedule. Under 91.137 the list of who gets in is short: relief aircraft, law enforcement, approved IFR traffic, flights to or from an airport inside it, news media with a flight plan flying above the relief aircraft, and a flight that can't go around for weather or terrain, after it tells the facility in the NOTAM. Looking at the fire isn't on it. Say the facts, offer the trade, and let the rules carry the weight.

The smoke cleared out on the eighth when the wind went northwest. On Saturday the 11th Abby planned a short dual cross country, Centennial to Rocky Mountain Metro and back, the long way around the west side of Denver under the Class B shelves. On the chart it looked like walking through a house in the dark where somebody keeps moving the furniture.
Your trip, your plan. After Tower lets you go, do you want flight following or not? I'm not voting.
On the kneeboard Jordan had the shelf floors along the route written down in a column, in MSL. She'd planned to cruise at 7,500. Some of the floors were not very far above that.
The trip to Rocky Mountain Metro winds under the Class B shelves. Which choice about ATC services fits?
A. Ask Tower to keep her on their frequency all the way to Rocky Mountain Metro.
B. Skip it. Under the shelves she doesn't need to talk to anyone, and the frequency is busy.
C. Request VFR traffic advisories from Denver Approach once she's out of Centennial's airspace.
D. Ask Approach for a clearance through the Class B, so she can fly straight over the top.

Tower hands her off. Denver Approach, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, five miles west of Centennial, six thousand eight hundred climbing seven thousand five hundred, request flight following to Rocky Mountain Metro. A woman's voice gives her a squawk code. Jordan reads it back and dials it in. Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, radar contact, five miles west of Centennial. Maintain VFR at or below seven thousand five hundred. Over Englewood: Traffic, two o'clock, three miles, eastbound, a Bonanza, seven thousand niner hundred. Jordan finds it. A dot that turns into an airplane. Traffic in sight, Niner One Echo. Abby writes FF on her kneeboard and draws a star next to it.

Exactly right. Flight following gives you radar traffic advisories, workload permitting, from the people who can see the traffic. It doesn't relieve you of see and avoid and it doesn't clear you into the Class B. It's a second set of eyes, and around Denver you want it.

On the way home, over Littleton, the radio went quiet. Not static. Nothing. Approach had told them to contact Centennial Tower, she'd dialed it in and called, and nothing came back. She called again. Her own voice came back to her in the headset the way it always did, and that was all, on a frequency that hadn't shut up for one second all morning.
She checked the volume. The squelch. Both headset plugs. The frequency, twice, out loud. Abby tried hers. Nothing.
Okay. This is real. What now?

Jordan squawked 7600. They found the edge of the Class D, then the tower cab, and she joined the downwind for 35R with her head turned toward it like she was trying to hear a conversation two tables over. Abeam the numbers, a light came out of the cab at them. Red. It didn't blink.
What does a steady red light gun signal require of an airplane in flight?
A. Leave the pattern and divert to an airport without a tower, where no clearance is needed.
B. Read it as airport unsafe, leave the area, and try another field nearby.
C. Give way to other traffic and keep circling in the pattern, watching for a green.
D. Land anyway. She's VFR, squawking 7600, and the tower knows exactly who she is.

She stretches the downwind out past where she'd normally turn, cab in the corner of the windshield, and a King Air she never heard on the radio slides in ahead of her and lands. Then all the way around again. Nobody to talk to, so she talks to Biscuit, under her breath, which Abby pretends not to hear. On base: green. Holding. She rocks the wings so hard Abby grabs the glare shield and says a word Jordan has never heard her say, and Jordan's still grinning like a dope when the mains squeak on. Marisol has the radio out of the panel in fifteen minutes flat. Connector on the back, half off, same deal as the ADS-B antenna in June. This panel's been shaking itself apart all summer. That night, alone, flashlight in her teeth, she goes through every plug behind it. In the morning there's a handheld radio in the seat back pocket and nobody mentions it. Later Abby tells her it was Danny's. He always kept it there. Marisol took it out in March.

That's it. Steady red in flight means give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Keep visual contact with the tower and wait for a steady green, which is your clearance to land. In flight by day you acknowledge by rocking your wings.

Wednesday evening Walt came by the hangar for his monthly logbook check, the way he'd done since May. He read every line of the last month, the cancellations included, with his glasses on the end of his nose, initialed the bottom of the page, and slid the logbook back.

Abby says you're working the Bravo. He set a pamphlet on the bench, the kind they hand out at safety meetings, with NASA on the front. A member of this club got a phone number from Denver Approach once. Climbing out east, right through the floor. Good pilot. Wasn't looking.
Jordan waited for the name. It didn't come.
You hear 'possible pilot deviation, advise you contact.' What do you do?
A. Let it go, keep flying the lesson, and wait to see if the FAA ever follows up.
B. Fly first, call the number once she's calm on the ground, and file with NASA.
C. Land, then call the number from the ramp right away, before the details fade.
D. Key up, explain what happened, and give the controller her side of it now.

Fly the airplane. Write the number down. Call once I'm on the ground, then file with NASA. Walt nods once. Ten days. Within ten days of the deviation, or of when you found out. NASA form. It doesn't stop the FAA from finding you did it, but if it was an honest mistake and you're clean for five years, nobody takes your certificate or your money. He taps the pamphlet. I've filed four in my life. Dispatch ones. Filing is what a professional does. Not filing is what somebody who thinks he's never wrong does.

Yep. That's the one. Acknowledge, fly the airplane, write the number down, get on the ground, then call. Then file an Aviation Safety Reporting System report with NASA within 10 days. A timely report on an inadvertent violation can waive the civil penalty or the suspension.
Decision twelve. Seven thousand eight hundred.
Saturday the 18th, clear, calm, the kind of morning that makes people buy airplanes. Abby said almost nothing on the walk out, which Jordan had learned meant a test.

Off 35R with a right turn east. Tower handed her to Denver Approach on the climb, and the controller gave her a squawk code. Jordan read it back, wrote it on her kneeboard, dialed it in, checked it, and the reply light blinked.
Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, radar contact, three miles east of Centennial.

Good. In the system. The reservoir was off the left wing, way too blue for Colorado, and she was half thinking about the practice area and the steep turns she'd botched last week and the 7,500 she was supposed to level at for them out in the practice area. She cranked in some trim. She looked at the reservoir again, because it was right there.
She was on with Approach, like always. Radar contact. In the system.
Something moved in the corner of her eye. Abby's finger, on the glass of the altimeter, just resting there. The nail was chipped.
Denver Approach said radar contact, and the climb hasn't stopped. What should Jordan do now?
A. Level off at exactly 8,000 and hold it until the GPS shows the shelf behind her.
B. Level off where she is and ask Denver Approach for a Class Bravo clearance.
C. Keep climbing a little. The shelf has to step up a few miles out this way.
D. Descend right away to 7,500 and stay well below the shelf floor.

She shoves the nose over and pulls a little power, and the altimeter winds down through 7,700 and 7,600 and settles on 7,500, where it should have been all along. Her palms are wet on the yoke. She stops looking at the reservoir. Abby lifts her finger off the glass and puts it back on her own knee. What'd Approach say when you checked in? Radar contact. And what's that mean? Jordan thinks about it longer than she'd like to. That they can see me. Yep. They'd have watched the whole thing. Out past the strut the wheat goes by in squares. After a while, in a voice Jordan hasn't heard out of her before, lower, almost kind: Two hundred feet. Everybody gets their two hundred feet once. That was yours.

Exactly right. Stop the climb and get back under the floor with a margin. The floor over Centennial is 8,000 MSL, and the shelves step down as you get closer to Denver International, so check every floor on your route on a current chart. "Radar contact" is not a Class B clearance. Stay below the floor unless you hear the words "cleared to enter the Class Bravo airspace."

They flew the steep turns at 7,500 that day, under the shelf, which turned out to be fine, and Jordan's were the best she'd flown. Abby wrote it up in the briefing room, 1.5 dual, and in the remarks put CLASS B AWARENESS, which made it sound like a seminar.

Jordan said she'd be a minute. She walked back out to Biscuit, sat in the left seat with the door open, and took two things out of her flight bag. Danny's old sectional, folded to the Denver panel. And the green notebook.
She'd skipped ahead once before. Today she did it again. She went looking, the way she'd look for one line in a chart that she knew had to be there, and found it about a third of the way through.

Danny's logbook, a page from August, eight years ago. August 9. KAPA local, 1.3. Gorgeous morning. Off 35R, right turn east. Approach gives me a squawk, I put it in, "radar contact," great, I'm in the system, I'm basically an airliner. Fiddling with the new GPS. Admiring the reservoir like a tourist. Approach comes back: "Cessna Niner One Echo, possible pilot deviation, advise you contact Denver TRACON at" and then a phone number, which I wrote on the back of my left hand with a grease pencil because I'm a professional. 8,300 feet. The floor over the field is 8,000. Called from the FBO, shaking. Guy was nice about it. Said "radar contact" means they can see you, and they sure did. Filed the NASA form that night. Walt helped and didn't say I told you so, which is how I knew it was bad. New rule: nothing above 7,500 until I'm past the shelf. Circled it on the chart so I can't miss it. Circled it again. And again.
Jordan read it twice. Then she unfolded his chart on her knees and looked at the red rings around the 80, three laps of them, and the pen going through the paper on the last one.

Off 35R, right turn east. Radar contact. The reservoir. She'd done it the same way. Not close to the same way. The same way, down to the thing she was looking at out the left window. He'd been a little over the line and she'd been a little under it, and the difference between those two mornings was a finger on the glass of the altimeter.

She'd spent four months either keeping away from everything that looked like him or trying to fly it exactly the way he would have. It hadn't occurred to her that she could do both at once, without meaning to, on a clear Saturday at seven thousand eight hundred feet. She sat there with that for a while.

Then she got a pen out of the door pocket and wrote on her kneeboard, under the strip of blue tape from the static port, in her own small handwriting: SHELF AT 80. SAY IT OUT LOUD BEFORE TAKEOFF. RADAR CONTACT ISN'T A YES. It wasn't his rule. His rule was 7,500 and a red pen. Hers was saying it out loud, which was the thing she did at work before every drug she pushed. She thought he'd have made fun of her for it. She thought he'd have been right to, a little.
Abby came out a few minutes later with her car keys in her teeth and her flight bag over one shoulder, saw the notebook, and stopped by the strut.

He told me about that one, she said. The week my first student failed a checkride. He showed up with breakfast burritos and told me it wasn't my fault, and then, I guess so I'd feel better, he told me the whole thing. The grease pencil, the phone call. He said the only pilots who never got a phone number were the ones who didn't fly enough to get one. She looked at the chart. He didn't tell me about the red circles.
He circled it three times. Jordan didn't look up from the chart.

Yeah. Abby nodded at the kneeboard. I like yours better. Same lesson. You can say yours out loud. She rapped the cowling twice with her knuckles on the way past, like it was a horse that had done fine, and went to find her car.

Jordan folded his chart back up along his creases. It took her four tries, and she was unreasonably proud of the fourth. She put it in the flight bag next to hers, with the red circles on the inside, where they'd keep.
